projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Arthur Jaklic was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran Arthur J. Jaklic. Mr. Jaklic served in the U.S. Navy with B Division. He served in the Pacific Theater on board the battleship U.S.S. Tennessee and his highest rank was machinist mate second class. I'm Tom Swope and this interview was recorded at Mr. Jaklic's home in metro Ohio on August 8th, 2004. Art was 84 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: In Cleveland. Collinwood area of Cleveland.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How old were you?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: I was 22 years old when I got - when I joined the Navy.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So in 19 -- do you have specific memories of December 7, 1941?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: Yes, Saturday night, went out after work because I was working nights. Now, let me see, December 7th, I'm trying to think back.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now that was Sunday so --

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: That was, that was Sunday and they didn't declare war until Monday.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: It was Saturday, I went out, came back and heard this news and I said, where is Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What did you personally think when you realized that we were in the war?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: Thought well, it could be anytime but in '41 I was working in a place where we made war materials or we worked on -- I tell you exactly what we worked on -- we worked on the turrets of M1 tanks. These machines would -- machine tanks. Machines needs turrets for the tanks. I think they made thousands of them because they got shot up. But I was -- six months, I wasn't able to leave because I was, you might say handcuffed to the job.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right, essential work.

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: And then once that was over, that's when I joined the Navy. And this fellow that was with me, we joined together and I went to boot camp up the Great Lakes and I guess he had a little college education and they took him and made an officer from him.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So that was sometime in 1942 then, when you joined up?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: Yeah, October 29th, I think.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember your first day of boot camp?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: No, I think there was a thousand guys -- a thousand naked guys going through the lines getting shots because we were in boot camp for 21 days, during that time we got 22 shots. And then home for a boot camp leave and back to Great Lakes to go to the machinist school and that was six months.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Anything you can tell me about that time, that training?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: The training, I thought it was pretty rough at the time but after a while I realized that this is something we need because I wasn't doing anything before, no exercise, no nothing. And so we got pretty well trimmed, lost a few pounds, but we got straightened out.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you were trained as a machinist?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: Machinist.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So what exactly would your responsibilities be then?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: Anything to do with the engineering division of a ship. And this we -- I started out as fireman third class which is on the bottom, very bottom, and then made my way up from there. I ended up as a second class machinist mate. And then when the war was over they offered me first class if I would stay and put the ship in moth balls. I said I came here to help you guys win this war, the war is over, adios. And I went home.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So was the Tennessee your first assignment then?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: The only, first one and only assignment.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So when did you go on board the Tennessee?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: I went on board in April 1943. And the ship was up in Birmington and it was being pretty modernized like I said and --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Glad you mentioned that, I don't think we had the tape running when you mentioned that. Briefly, what did they do to the Tennessee after Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: They took all the figures off the top of the ship except the main battery which is the 14-inch guns and they replaced them with -- didn't replace the 14-inch guns that stayed there because that -- they're big because the barrels are 50-feet long and there was three barrels in each -- three guns in each turret. We had four turrets. And we had 14-inch 38s and believe me this was an Oerlikon gun which is designed by Oerlikon in -- Oerlikon was selling guns to both sides, the Germans and the Americans. I found that out later because at one time the company I worked for was -- belonged to Oerlikon Burley.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oerlikon, where were they from?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: Switzerland.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So a Swiss company was making arms for both sides?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: Both sides, yeah. And so they put 40 millimeter quads on, which was four barrels in each station you might say, and there was loaders, one loader for each barrel and ammunition passes from there and these were fixed ammunition and there was four shots to each clip and every time they grabbed one they put it right into the barrel and shoot him out. They were about, I'd say 15-inches long and about an inch-and-a-half in diameter, that's what I would say because they were 40 millimeter. But I would like to tell you about the three times that I got on my knees to ask the Lord for help. The first time, after we -- the ship was in -- all fixed up, we went out for a trial run in the Wanafooka(ph) Straits which is more calm than Lake Erie is at times and it was beautiful. We thought it was nothing to it. Until on a Saturday evening we went out to sea and we hit ground swells. These ground swells had valleys, I would say 40-50 feet deep and although the ship was 630-feet long and I think it was 90 -- 110 feet wide, we rode around like a cork and I got seasick. Seasick, I was seasick for four days. I had to stand watch, couldn't get away from that. Sick as a dog, like to die, I said Lord, kill me if this isn't going to end, but four days later it ended, and after that I was okay. And --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you ever get seasick again after that?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: No. Never did.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, really?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: I think now if I went out to the lake somewhere in a boat I'd probably get seasick.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now, yeah. But back then --

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: Back then, no, you get used to it. But the next time, now I don't remember now when we went through the typhoon if it was before the Battle of the Surigao Straits or after, but it was the worst typhoon that they had in years. I know the Navy had lost a lot of planes especially on those small flattops where they lost maybe 700 planes all together. And the typhoon -- I don't know if you heard about the typhoon they had out there. We lost destroyers, complete destroyers and there's 250 men on them. And we were guaranteed to go 47 degrees. We went 45 degrees, so you know how rough it was. We had -- everything had to be tied down, chained down, or wired down so we wouldn't lose it. On the outside they passed the word: do not go outside on deck unless you absolutely have to. And when we went places we had to hang onto something, but that only lasted a couple of days.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And those were sometime in 1945, is that right?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: I don't remember if it was '44 or no, I think it was-- it might have been '44 because that was the same year that we went to the Battle of Surigao Straits. Now, I don't know why the Japanese Navy came after us because there was, there was two battleships this was -- if I could remember the date, October 25th, 1944. There was two battleships, two cruisers, and four destroyers came after us, they figured they were gonna -- because in the early part of the war their Navy was terrific because they sank a dozen of our cruisers in the Pacific and this time they came after us there -- we had six battleships, nine cruisers, and about 20 destroyers. But these were all vintage ships because the ship I was on was on the -- put on the boards in 1915, it wasn't built until -- during the first world war and the Navy didn't accept the ship until 1921. But during that time the ship was mostly in the -- partly in the Pacific and partly in the Atlantic but it ended up in Pearl Harbor, December 7th because at that time it still could go through the Panama Canal. Once they got through from Birmington and had the new blisters put on it, we couldn't go through the Panama Canal. We were too wide. But we were able to hold 1,700,000 gallons of fuel. That's enough to fuel us for one month and fuel two destroyers. If you ever see destroyers being fuelled in rough weather, that is something. I mean really rough.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have any incidents or any trouble when you tried to do that with fuel?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: We did that and one time the hose came off, off of the ship and the one side of that destroyer was just covered with fuel oil and this fuel oil was black, almost completely black, because it had to be heated before we even burn it. But we used to use about 85,000 gallons a day to steam, so it, it was pretty big -- of course one of the reasons why we didn't tip over during that typhoon is because we had a draft of 32 feet which is pretty -- a lot, a lot of draft for a ship of course it was __ was 41,000 tons. Actually when you come right down to it, it's displaced 41,000 tons of water. That's how they did it. And, yeah, now coming back to the Battle of Surigao Straits, I guess the Japanese fleet figured they had thumbs up on it. And they came after us. We began in general quarters at 2 o'clock in the morning on the 25th and commenced firing at five minutes to three and at eight minutes after three we had all those ships sunk. We were 11 and a-half miles away, when we began firing. They didn't have a chance because we fired 69 rounds, only one ship fired more guns then we did at that time. One of the ships only fired once and they had some problem, they couldn't fire anymore but with all the ships together the Japanese didn't have a chance. In 13 minutes they were gone. And the bad part, or I think was the sad part of this was the next morning they sent in destroyers and PT boats to pick up the survivors. They didn't want to be saved. They wanted to die for the Emperor. So we never, we never had a prisoner of war on the ship. We were asked to take one on the ship, but we turned it down.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Your crew turned it down or your commander turned it down?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: No, our commander turned it down.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: I have no reason why, I guess we only had one brig and they didn't want to fool around with this Jap, so that was it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But they would fight, when they went and tried to rescue them and they would fight and they wouldn't --

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: They didn't want to be rescued. Yeah, this, I tell you we had some good times on the ship we had some good leave, shore leave and sometimes it was rough. I remember the time when it was really -- got hot they passed the word, the temperature's 125 out in the sun. Don't go out unless you absolutely have to. And I remember the time when we had a problem in engineering division, as a matter of fact I was in B division, that's the reason why I was -- there was only four machinist mates in the B Division. All the rest were water tenors because they took care of the boilers. We had eight boilers on the ship and we took care of the machinery that forced the air down to the fire room because the fire -- the boilers had to be under air pressure to function properly. You had to have a certain amount of air, a certain amount of oil, so that you don't get any smoke out of the smokestack. And they had a man on watch all the time, course they took turns at smoke watch, always checking out which fire room would be smoking and they'd tell them and they'd change it either more air or less air. And one of the things I remember is we'd get on the ?sock pair? phones and listen to the smoke watch and during the Battle of Surigao Straits he says - he says it's like Fourth of July. He says those things get red hot going through the air. Now these shells that we fired were 1,500 pounds a piece. We fired -- always fired three guns at a time each salvo. We started with three at the beginning and after that it was all six guns salvos and always fired broadside never on forward or aft. They tried that years ago and all they do is buckle the deck.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Because of the --

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: The recoil. All those guns went back six feet, the ship also moved at the recoil and each shell had to have 28 pounds of powder behind it to send that out there, but this was not really powder. It was cordite, which really isn't a gun powder, but it's explosive. What else can I tell you?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, whatever else you want to tell me about life on board ship.

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: Oh, well I was in the engineer's tool room. I had to stand watches until I got to be in charge of the engineer's tool room which is the last few months on the ship and then I didn't stand any watches and from that I was nice, really nice. I had friends all across the ship like the bake shop. That was the best place to have a friend. We had a fellow that left -- I'm trying to forg-- I don't remember now, he was a Polish fellow, Poland, he left Poland five days before Hitler got there. Couldn't read or write English, he'd speak it a little, but he would get mail and I'd read his mail and write his letters for him. And he'd tell me if I wanted anything from the bake shop, I got it. I went up there and I'd say, how about a pie? He'd give me four of them. Or some biscuits, he'd give me a whole tray of them. That wasn't hard to take because sometimes the -- I remember one time we had bread. The flour had some bugs in it. And they passed the word when you see bugs in the bread, put it up to the light and you see dark spots in it, just poke them out because those were bugs. And we couldn't help it that was it. But --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But overall was the food pretty good on the ship?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: Well, I wouldn't say it's gourmet food, but you lived by it anyway. The part that I didn't like was you get these cups, they didn't have any handles, they come out of the scullery, so hot you almost burn your fingers. Then you put hot coffee in on top of that and we had to drink it. Either that or let it cool off. But almost every station had its own coffee pot. And you were allowed to have canned milk and sugar and coffee which it didn't cost us anything.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How about you said you and your buddies, what did anything you do to pass the time or for entertainment or anything?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: Yeah. Played pinochle, that's one of the things and I played poker once. In ten minutes I lost 25 bucks. I said this game is not for me. I never played it again, never. Even today I don't play it. But pinochle, yes. That's about it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have to go through the initiation ceremony when you crossed the equator?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: It so happened that I was lucky when -- we went over a couple times, but the first time we were on our way to the enemy so we had no initiation. So the second time we went over we were already initiated automatically because we didn't have to take the initiation some of them did have because I know the captain in one place was the executive officer and your executive officer had to be and he got in on it. And it was just like any other ship had the same thing on it. And I could show you pictures of the initiation if I can find it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I've heard some stories about it.

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you involved in any other major actions when you were on board the ship?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: Which kind of actions?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Major actions or any actions at all that you'd want to talk about?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: Oh yes, we were in 15 of them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Fifteen, wow, anything else of those that you want to tell me about?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: Well, it's kind of hard to say because the first major action that we were in was up in the Aleutian Islands, in Alaska. We were up there for three months and we fired on Adak and Kiska and there was another lesser island that --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Attu?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: Attu was the other one we fired on there and we were there for three months but during that time only saw the one sun once because it's so foggy up there. And the Japanese planes come up there and the cold from Alaska and it was just the -- and then we had an admiral while we were up there and I don't remember what this admiral, but I think it was Kingman, yeah, and he wanted to have admiral's inspection. So we were in the Bering Straits at that time. Snowing, had all our just blues on, had our jackets on and there it was having an admiral's inspection, which I think was stupid. There's something that they had stupid, but it all comes out to one thing. Do you want to have control of the men? That was the thing.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: But, we had four admirals on ship at one time or another. And our ship was generally the flag ship, as a matter of fact Oldendorf, Jesse Oldendorf was the admiral when we won the Battle of Surigao Straits and he's the one that figured out what we should do before and had all the other ships line up so that we were facing -- not going, going sideways according to the Japanese coming after us. But, the Japanese didn't have a chance at that time. We didn't give them a chance. I think we owed 'em that. But like I said I want to get you some pictures on here -- oh yes, one of the things that the Tennessee was only two battleships received Navy citations during World War II, the Tennessee was one of them. The other one was, I think the Pennsylvania. And we got that because of our gunnery, main battery gunnery. Many times we were called back a second time, a third time, sometimes a fourth time until I get to Iwo Jima to -- because we were very accurate. I mean right now -- even during the civil, during the pre-wartime, the Tennessee would get E's for excellence in their - in their shooting.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you supported the invasions of Iwo Jima --

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Okinawa?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: As a matter of fact __, Kiska, Tarawa, Kwajalein, Eniwetok, Kavieng, Saipan, Guam, Tinian, Angaur, Leyte, Battle of Surigao Straits, Iwo Jima, and Okinawa, every one of them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Anything come to mind when you think about those?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: No, not really. Because I remember the time we were in the Philippines. We were anchored and a Japanese plane went by. He was so close to me, I could see the pilot. But he dropped a fish in one of the cruisers and it happened to be the sister ship of the cruiser that the General was on. Came back to -- from the Philippines.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: McCarthur?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: McCarthur. And it just so happens that these -- hit the sister ship of this cruiser, I think it was the Honolulu, but I'm not sure. That was -- it was that close and this guy, this Japanese plane got away and everybody was shooting at it. I happened to be standing under the guns the five inch guns and you know those shells are about that long with powder about that long. Never hurt him. Never hurt him.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Many kamikazes?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: We got hit -- I can't -- I don't -- have to look it up to see where -- what day we got hit. We got -- it was seven kamikazes come after us. And we shot down, well, we shot them all down but the seventh one was already on its way to hit one side and it dropped a bomb, 500-hundred pound bomb, and gasoline was the worse thing, it did a lot of damage. We lost 27 men that day. And all that was washed the plane off the side. I still have a piece of aluminum from the plane that I picked up off the deck, and I still have it today. But that was bad. That was the worst I ever had. Well, we were pretty fortunate, while I was on the ship we only lost 44 men altogether, which was great for us. Because we got hit at Saipan, or rather we were at Saipan, we got hit from Tinian. The Japanese had taken the six-inch guns from Singapore and put them on these other islands because they knew eventually that we were going to go after these islands and we took three shells, one at the water line, one in the ward room and one in the five-inch gun. And it happened to hit at a place where it was -- the only place that was not armor plated. Right where the slide is, they had a brass slide where they elevate the barrel that's where the shot went in. Killed all twelve guys in the gun and that was it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get much mail on board ship?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: Occasionally, yeah. Most of the time it would be a lot of mail at one time then you wouldn't get it for four or five months. You wouldn't get anything. Then it would happen again. Yeah, this is the number of -- of operations we had against the enemy.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And you were on beginning with the Aleutians?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: With the Aleutians, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So the only World War II that you missed with the Tennessee was when you went there on Pearl Harbor.

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: Pearl Harbor. That's right. That happened before I got on.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum. So you enjoyed the Navy life?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: Sometimes, yes. Sometimes it was really good. Went to Pearl Harbor a few times. Went to Honolulu. And one of the things that I did enjoy at one time -- at a place -- the Navy had a place out, oh, maybe 30 miles from Pearl City and we went there by narrow gauge railroad. Called Nanakuli -- and go there, swim all you want, did anything you want for three days. If you wanted to go to church, you go to church, if not, you didn't have to. Do whatever you want. Just let it wring -- just wring it out. And I just took it easy, which was good. We only had four days, but while I was in Honolulu, it was my drinking days. And I did a little drinking there. One of the things we always wanted to do is get a good meal and get something to drink because we couldn't drink on the ship. At times -- I remember one time we had -- this was a dark of night, not only at night, but they had smoke to cover the entire ship's motion and we had a supply ship hit us and go right into the -- in the side and went as far as the one locker. It just happened to be the beer locker, where they kept the beer. And believe me that was locked. The only time we ever got -- that I remember -- got beer is we went ashore to a small island to play ball and this island I don't think was ten acres. And it wasn't three feet high off the water. We played ball and had warm beer to drink. And that was it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was there much trading with the ground forces for souvenirs and things?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: Yeah. I tried to get some things when I was in Tokyo, which is about two weeks after the war was over. And I couldn't, just couldn't get anything. But I know a friend of mine who was in the Army and he was in Europe first and sent to the Pacific and he traded a Japanese family there for a set of pearls for a bag of sugar. He found out later these pearls were worth almost a 1,000 dollars but it -- all it cost him was a bag of sugar. Now when we got -- when the war was over we took -- we went to, not to the main island of Japan, but one of the lesser islands which I think was - oh, I have to see a map to tell you where it is. But I'm looking in here to see where, what island it was. Because we met a woman there, or not a woman, a young woman, only twelve years old who was raised in San Francisco. She spoke English. But there was another woman who must have been in her thirties and she had a child with her and they had a kind of a thing and the child in the bag behind them that -- on -- carried on there shoulder. And this woman smiled and all you could see is gold. She had uppers and lowers complete gold. I'm trying to think of the name of the island that we were on. Because we were there to accept the surrender of -- Wakayama.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wakayama?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: Yes, as a matter of fact this is the Wakayama surrender. The generals came aboard the ship and that was it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was that soon after the surrender in Tokyo Bay?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: Yes. That was almost I think the same day.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The same day?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And do you remember any big celebrations on V-J Day?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: No, we were -- we still had to work and do our work but we were glad it was over.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How about when you heard the atomic bomb had been dropped did you --

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: We were 350 miles away from the second bomb that was dropped.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Nagasaki?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: Nagasaki. But we didn't see anything. We were too far -- we were beyond the circ -- of the earth, the circumference. Oh, this is the girl that was from San Francisco.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. That's a great picture.

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: Yeah. This is pretty good and then when we went to Tokyo, of course, I was only in Tokyo twice.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What were the people like when you were there in Japan?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: Very quiet. They weren't hostile but they did tell you never go alone because you don't know what's going to happen. Make sure that you have either four or five, six people together whenever you went. But in Tokyo we'd go and walk through the town and through the city rather. There was houses, and you go another block, nothing but rubble. And most of that was rubble in Tokyo because they took a beating -- dropped a lot of firebombs in Tokyo. And the only -- we did see the Japanese, one battleship that was left of the Jap-- Japan -- when the war was over. They were afraid to take it out 'cause - yeah, this is, this is -- gives you a picture of what the -- what it looked like when they took --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Devastation in Tokyo, yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: Yeah. I'm glad of one thing that we didn't have to fight to get on Japan's mainland.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: Because it was -- it would have been rough. I think that was one of the best things that the President did was drop the bomb. Course the Jap-- Japan lost a lot of people but it saved a lot of us.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Could any of the guys, could you comprehend what the atomic bomb was?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: No. We had to -- since our engineer's tool room was also in the same place as the B Division office, we were the first ones that would get any news from the -- that would come out of Washington or from the -- actually from Honolulu because that was the center of the -- engagements in the Pacific. And we learned about that and how -- what they did later on. That was a well kept secret till they dropped it. Coming back -- going home since we couldn't go through the Panama Canal, we went around the world. With three battleships, a couple of cruisers and some destroyers and we stopped -- we started at Tokyo and went to Singapore And at Singapore I had a watch that wasn't keep -- wouldn't keep good time but I met a couple of Australian soldiers who wanted the watches. They said they didn't have any watches in Australia. They wanted them so I traded them. What did I get? I traded for two guns. A .30 Colt automatic and a German pistol and didn't keep them. The next time we dropped anchor we had a -- I sold chances for a dollar a piece for each minute of the clock. And when the anchor was dropped that time was recorded. That's the time that somebody got -- they want the gun. Hey, those watches cost me nothing -- that watch cost me nothing but I got about 120 dollars off the guns.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Very good.

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: So I didn't do so bad. Because you know we had an armory on the ship and I couldn't -- they wouldn't give me any ammunition for the .32 automatic. You're not supposed to have a gun to begin with. Because when we were in port I would have to go to the armory to pick up a .45 to carry for our armored -- for the third deck watch. And they wouldn't give me any .32 automatic but they had all kinds of guns on the ship. They had browning automatics, BARs, they had machine guns. They had 306's, all kinds of rifles - but, that was it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So what other stops did you make along the way as you came back home?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: Oh, I didn't finish that. We went to Singapore and then from Singapore we went through the Malacca Straits and we went to Salon which today is not Salon. It's called Sri Lanka now and we were in Colombo and that was the first time I saw elephants pulling wagons when we were there in Colombo and not only that it was the first time I saw a steam - now, it wasn't a train it was a more like a truck. It was hauling four or five trailers behind it right down the road, right down the street and to me it was unique because you didn't see any of that at home. And that was a pretty good place and then the last place we stopped before we came home was at Cape Town, South Africa. And that was pretty good place because the people there spoke English and of course before we went ashore they said there's a lot of mixed marriages in Cape Town, make sure you don't date a black or dark woman because then you might get in trouble. So we made sure we didn't -- I didn't date any women then. But I tell you one thing we went to a family -- went to a movie and met these people at a movie there. And then we went to their house and had dinner and I think the next day we went ashore we brought them some cigarettes because they said the cigarettes they had were 50 in a pack of cigarettes and they gave me a pack and they tasted terrible compared to American cigarettes. I was a smoker at that time. And so we gave them cigarettes and they gave us a meal, which was good. And it happened to see a picture, a man had a picture of a woman on the table and she -- completely naked. It was his wife. They thought nothing of it. Which was of course a little different than in the United States.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: But that was about it and then from there we came home and we came to Philadelphia. And when the Navy yard and then in 1959 they took the Tennessee apart. They took the guns out. They kept the guns and cut the other stuff up for scrap. Guess where they sold the scrap to?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Probably Japan, right?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: Japan. Back in the sixties when Hondas were coming to the United States, that's where the steel was.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The Tennessees were coming back.

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: There was a lot of steel there because our protective dig on top was nine-inches thick and it was 400-feet long and I would say it was 90-feet wide at the widest spot because that was cover the engineering space so the engineering space wouldn't get damaged. This is something they didn't have on flattops. Flattops didn't have that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So what was your reunion with your family like when you got back after the war?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: Very happy. I went back to the Great Lakes and got discharged from Great Lake and came back and I think a week later I went back to work. To the place I left. And from that time on it was one thing after another.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any other vivid memories come to mind about the war?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: Really, not really. I think -- I did a lot -- stood a lot of watches believe me, because you're four on and eight off all the time. That goes on one year after another, never stops.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You think we covered it?

sp.speaker: Arthur Jaklic
sp.p: I think that just about covers it.
